rail_guard.text: Whitby Station. The end of the line, quite literally, or the start of it, depending on whether you have a bag of chips.
All aboard! The trains go everywhere you have been. Mind the gap, and the herring gull.

wby_chipper.text: Haddock, chips, mushy peas, bread and butter, and a pot of tea. Yorkshire law, that is. The haddock is from the boat you just saw.
Watch your chips. The gulls here are professionals. They don't dive. They wait until you look at the sea.

wby_jeweller.text: Whitby jet is fossilised monkey-puzzle wood, nearly 180 million years old. You can carve it, and it takes a lovely polish, and it will pull a tiny scrap of paper to itself if you rub it.
Queen Victoria wore it in mourning, so every lady in the land wanted it. At the peak there were two hundred jet workshops in this little town. Now there are some. I'm one.

wby_goth.text: Whitby Goth Weekend! Twice a year, thousands of us arrive in black velvet and top hats and walk up the 199 steps, because that is what Dracula would do.
The locals are delighted. A top hat on a seagull is a statement. A seagull wearing it is a different matter.

wby_skipper.text: The Endeavour was built here in 1764 as a coal ship called the Earl of Pembroke. The navy bought it, renamed it, and sent Captain Cook round the world in it. A Whitby collier, circling the globe!
Colliers were broad and flat-bottomed, so they could sit on the mud at low tide without falling over. A good ship for the unknown.

wby_bard.text: Caedmon was a cowherd who was too shy to sing at feasts. He left one night, had a dream, and woke up able to sing in his own language. He sang, in English, about creation. It's the oldest English poem we have.
I have written nine hundred poems and a limerick. The limerick is the one people remember.
